q-126569.name: Question 1
q-126569.problem:
Given that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $F(x,y)=⟨y(x-1),\,x(y-1)⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
q-126569.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120201/assets/b95320928a5e7482f9ba2b8bb1d1499950710545b4c7273b7f70dfe5ab8c84b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=y(x-1)$ and $Q(x,y)=x(y-1),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x-1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=y-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}y(x-1)\,dx+x(y-1)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((y-1)-(x-1))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(y-x)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{4}{r}^{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-126569.html:
Question 1
?

Given that ∮CF⋅dr=∫02π∫04AAAAAAAAdrdθ, where F(x,y)=⟨y(x−1),x(y−1)⟩ and C is the circle x2+y2=16 oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?

a
r(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
b
r2
c
r2(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)
d
rcos⁡(2θ)
e
r2cos⁡(2θ)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as

∮CF⋅dr=∮Cy(x−1)dx+x(y−1)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=y(x−1) and Q(x,y)=x(y−1), we obtain

∂P∂y=x−1,∂Q∂x=y−1.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮Cy(x−1)dx+x(y−1)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D((y−1)−(x−1))dA=∬D(y−x)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as

Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤4,0≤θ≤2π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D(y−x)dA=∬Δ(rsin⁡θ−rcos⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫02π∫04r2(sin⁡θ−cos⁡θ)drdθ.

q-41469.name: Question 2
q-41469.problem:
Given that 

$$
{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1$ oriented counterclockwise, what is the missing part of the equation?
q-41469.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120201/assets/459a51f3c408a9c647b3be6b978267a6ce724e747118fbe897275c370d2bb6d6.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(1-2y)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(1-2\cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}r-2{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

q-126708.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120201/assets/e54e2dc5c314ed1dda6ef9c60db5c5df3058ba120afec42bddbabc2622c3ae98.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Given that $F(x,y)=⟨x+y,\,-xy⟩,$ which of the following is equivalent to ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr\,?$
q-126708.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(-xy)\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120201/assets/e1c053e1cc4b4304c1302da2c57278200931b84e4ba687269d0ea89a99b523b8.png)

Since $P(x,y)=x+y$ and $Q(x,y)=-xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-y.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(-xy)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 6,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

 

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(-y-1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}(-r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -1)\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{6}(-{r}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -r)\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

a

c

EXPLANATION

∮CF⋅dr=∮C(x+y)dx+(−xy)dy.

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=x+y and Q(x,y)=−xy, we obtain

∂P∂y=1,∂Q∂x=−y.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(x+y)dx+(−xy)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(−y−1)dA=∬D(−y−1)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤6,π2≤θ≤2π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

q-126516.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120201/assets/bc0660c37a6658635311a9a973ae3f4802740622a0b35ade22d6050ce648efa6.png)

Consider the path $C$ shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral 

$$
{∮}_{C}({y}^{3}-x)\,dx+({x}^{3}+{e}^{1/y})\,dy\,?
$$
q-126516.worked_solution:
Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120201/assets/7724df0035511419dcb5117ba8aa337380325af22ee235d206a954aa12c62fe9.png)

Since $P(x,y)={y}^{3}-x$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{3}+{e}^{1/y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({y}^{3}-x)\,dx+({x}^{3}+{e}^{1/y})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that 

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, we can write our double integral as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }\,{\int }_{0}^{1}3{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,dr\,d\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the path C shown above. Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral ∮C(y3−x)dx+(x3+e1/y)dy?

EXPLANATION

Green's theorem states that ∮CPdx+Qdy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA.

In our case, the region D and its boundary C satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

Since P(x,y)=y3−x and Q(x,y)=x3+e1/y, we obtain

∂P∂y=3y2,∂Q∂x=3x2.

Applying Green's theorem, we get

∮C(y3−x)dx+(x3+e1/y)dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA=∬D(3x2−3y2)dA=∬D3(x2−y2)dA.

Now, notice that the region D can be represented in polar coordinates as Δ={(r,θ):0≤r≤1,−π2≤θ≤π}.

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that ∬Df(x,y) dA=∬Δ f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r drdθ.

Therefore, we can write our double integral as

∬D3(x2−y2)dA=∬Δ3(r2cos2⁡θ−r2sin2⁡θ)rdrdθ=∫−π/2π∫013r3cos⁡(2θ)drdθ.

q-109119.name: Question 5
q-109119.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨{x}^{2}y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x,4-x{y}^{2}⟩$ and $C$ is the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ oriented counterclockwise.
q-109119.worked_solution:
First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({x}^{2}y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx+(4-x{y}^{2})\,dy.
$$

Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

In our case, the region $D$ and its boundary $C$ satisfy the conditions of Green's theorem:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14120201/assets/09a69771617d73af6e4a1a42720223951e2e6edeb71a8df4d12aeb1bc22031aa.png)

Now, since 

$$
P(x,y)={x}^{2}y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,Q(x,y)=4-x{y}^{2},
$$

we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}={x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({x}^{2}y-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\,dx+(4-x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-{y}^{2}-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}-({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =-4[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =-4(2\pi -0) \\  & =-8\pi \end{aligned}
$$

P(x,y)={sin}^{3}⁡x-{y}^{3},\,Q(x,y)={y}^{4}+{x}^{3},
$$

 we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-3{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({sin}^{3}⁡x-{y}^{3})\,dx+({y}^{4}+{x}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3{x}^{2}-(-3{y}^{2}))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

The change of variables formula for plane polar coordinates states that

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Finally, we can calculate our double integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}3({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{81}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{243}{4}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{243}{4}(2\pi -0) \\  & =\frac{243\text{ }\,\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
